# Factors, Strings, and Dates {#sec-types} Numeric columns misbehave loudly: a value that should be a number and is not stops the analysis within the minute. Text, categories, and dates fail the other way. Take the first number in each HF-HOME discharge medication string as its dose in milligrams, and 3,701 of the 15,530 doses written in milligrams or micrograms are wrong, with no error: `Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg` becomes 0 mg, and `digoxin 125 mcg` becomes 125 mg, a thousand times the prescribed dose. A date parsed under the wrong convention is still a date, and a factor with an unintended reference level still fits a model. Each produces a result rather than an error, and the result looks exactly as it should; this chapter makes each of those failures loud. ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.* [Phil Karlton]{.smallcaps}, *attributed* (c. 1996) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where this chapter sits: giving text, categories, and dates their types is part of the Wrangle stage, between the raw export and the derived analytic data.](14-types_files/figure-html/fig-types-pipeline-1.png){#fig-types-pipeline fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram of the analysis pipeline: six stages in order (Plan, Acquire, Wrangle, Analyze, Report, Share) above two bands that run under every stage (Version control and Environment). Highlighted for this chapter: Wrangle.' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note title='In this chapter'} **Reading time.** About 30 minutes. **You'll need.** @sec-acquisition for reading the HF-HOME files, and @sec-wrangling for the per-site recodes this chapter builds on. The code uses: ```r library(tidyverse) # includes forcats, stringr, and lubridate ``` **You'll be able to.** - Turn a variable coded several ways into a factor with a declared level set and reference level, and verify the recode. - Extract drug, dose, unit, and frequency from free-text dosing strings, and count what a careless pattern gets wrong. - Parse dates written in several formats, and detect the values that a multi-format parser may silently misread. - Choose between a period and a duration, and between `with_tz()` and `force_tz()`, for a given question. **Outline.** - [Factors: categories with a declared level set](#sec-types-factors) - [Strings: structure from free text](#sec-types-strings) - [Dates: formats, ambiguity, and time](#sec-types-dates) - [Worked example: a typed patient table](#sec-types-worked) ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Skip ahead?'} If these answers come quickly, skip to the next chapter. The answers are in @sec-quiz-answers-14. 1. Why has `stringsAsFactors = FALSE` been the default since R 4.0, and what problems did the old default cause? 2. What does `stringr::str_detect()` return, and how does it differ from `stringr::str_extract()`? 3. Given `c('2026-04-23', '04/23/2026', 'April 23, 2026')`, write one `lubridate` call that parses all three into dates, and say what could go wrong if a fourth value were `'03/04/2026'`. ::: ## Factors: categories with a declared level set {#sec-types-factors} A character vector is flexible: any value, any order, any new value later. A factor is constrained: a fixed set of levels, a defined order, and a first level that a model treats as the reference. For analysis the constraints are correct, because the model needs the level set and the reference. For cleaning and joining they are a hazard, because a new or misspelled value has nowhere to go. The decision is therefore not whether to use factors but *when* to convert, and @fig-factor-timing gives the answer this chapter argues for (Habit 7). ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-factor-timing %%| fig-alt: "Left-to-right chain. Read, clean and recode, and join %%| all stay in character type. A highlighted node marks where to %%| convert to factor, setting the reference level deliberately. %%| From there the chain branches to Model and to Plot, both %%| working in factor type." %%| fig-cap: "Where to convert. Character is the safe type through %%| reading, cleaning, and joining, because a new or misspelled %%| value is merely a new string rather than an invalid level. %%| Factor is the correct type at modeling and plotting, because %%| the model needs a fixed level set and a declared reference." flowchart LR R["Read
character"] --> C["Clean and recode
character"] C --> J["Join
character"] J --> X["Convert here
factor, reference level
set deliberately"] X --> M["Model
factor"] X --> P["Plot
factor, ordered
by fct_reorder"] ``` The generic tour of `forcats` is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 16], and the full verb list is in the cheat sheet at the end of this chapter. The sections below start from a problem in the HF-HOME export and reach for the verb that solves it. ### A variable coded four ways The case report form (CRF) export records sex as `F`/`M` at two sites, `Female`/`Male` at one, `f`/`m` at another, and `2`/`1` at Site D, whose codebook maps 1 to male and 2 to female. @sec-wrangling recoded these with `case_when()`; `forcats::fct_collapse()` does the same in the vocabulary of levels: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome") crf_raw <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character()) |> mutate(site_raw = site, site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)), patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0")) crf_typed <- crf_raw |> mutate(sex = fct_collapse(sex, F = c("F", "Female", "f", "2"), M = c("M", "Male", "m", "1")) |> fct_relevel("F", "M")) levels(crf_typed$sex) #> [1] "F" "M" crf_typed |> count(site, raw = crf_raw$sex, sex) #> # A tibble: 10 × 4 #> site raw sex n #> #> 1 Site A F F 308 #> 2 Site A M M 392 #> 3 Site B Female F 268 #> 4 Site B Male M 303 #> 5 Site C f F 225 #> 6 Site C m M 273 #> 7 Site D 1 M 230 #> 8 Site D 2 F 143 #> 9 Site E F F 122 #> 10 Site E M M 168 ``` ::: The collapsed levels come out in the order of the raw codes they absorbed, so `fct_relevel()` states the order you want. More important, `fct_collapse()` leaves any code you did not list as a level of its own, without a warning. That is why the levels are printed, and why the verification below asserts them: an unexpected code, such as `U` arriving next quarter, then stops the script instead of becoming a third sex. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} The running study ships the clean `demographics.csv`, so the recode can be checked against an answer key: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} demographics <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"), col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE) key <- match(crf_typed$patient_id, demographics$patient_id) stopifnot( identical(levels(crf_typed$sex), c("F", "M")), !anyNA(key), all(as.character(crf_typed$sex) == demographics$sex[key]) ) ``` ::: A real export has no answer key; there, the cross-tabulation above, read line by line against each site's codebook, is the check. ::: ### Declaring the level set The site labels arrive in fifteen spellings of five sites. A factor built with `factor()` and no levels accepts all fifteen, in alphabetical order. A factor built with the levels the protocol names turns every other spelling into `NA`, which an assertion can catch: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} site_levels <- paste("Site", LETTERS[1:5]) nlevels(factor(crf_raw$site_raw)) #> [1] 15 crf_typed <- crf_typed |> mutate(site = factor(site, levels = site_levels)) stopifnot(!anyNA(crf_typed$site)) fct_count(crf_typed$site) #> # A tibble: 5 × 2 #> f n #> #> 1 Site A 700 #> 2 Site B 571 #> 3 Site C 498 #> 4 Site D 373 #> 5 Site E 290 ``` ::: Declared levels also fix the order of every table and figure. Use `fct_infreq()` or `fct_reorder()` when the order should follow the data, as in a bar chart sorted by count; keep the protocol's order when the reader will look for a site by name. ### The reference level `randomization.csv` records the arm as `Usual care` or `Home health`. Left to `factor()`, the levels are alphabetical, so `Home health` becomes the reference and the model reports the effect of usual care: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} randomization <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"), col_types = cols(.default = col_character())) outcomes <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "outcomes.csv"), col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE) trial <- randomization |> inner_join(outcomes, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") levels(factor(trial$arm)) #> [1] "Home health" "Usual care" fit_default <- glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial, data = trial |> mutate(arm = factor(arm))) fit_declared <- glm(event_30d ~ arm, family = binomial, data = trial |> mutate(arm = factor( arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")))) coef(fit_default)[2] #> armUsual care #> 0.145559 coef(fit_declared)[2] #> armHome health #> -0.145559 ``` ::: The two coefficients have the same size and opposite signs. Neither is wrong; a reader who assumes the usual-care arm is the comparison reads the first one's direction backwards. Declare the reference in the cleaning script, in writing, where a reviewer can see it. Whether the estimate is distinguishable from zero is a question for the analysis plan (@sec-analysis-plan), not for the factor. ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} > **Context.** My model is `glm(event_30d ~ arm + site + sex, > family = binomial)`. The levels of each factor, as printed by > `levels()`, are below, with one sentence from the protocol naming > the control arm. > > **Constraints.** Do not refit or change the formula. Set levels > with `factor(..., levels = )` or `forcats::fct_relevel()` in the > data-cleaning step, not inside the model call. > > **Criteria.** For each factor, say which level is the reference > now, which it should be and why, and write the code that sets it. > Then state in one sentence what the `arm` coefficient will mean > after the change, including its sign convention. *Failure mode.* Models assert that 'the first level is the reference' without checking which level is first, or set the reference inside the formula with `relevel()` where the next model in the script does not inherit it. *Check.* Run `levels()` on each factor after the change, refit, and confirm that the coefficient's name (`armHome health`) names the treated arm. Send level names, never rows (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### Factors in joins and arithmetic A `dplyr` join on factor keys compares labels, not the integer codes behind them, so the rows match correctly. Two subtler things happen, both without a warning: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} a <- tibble(site = factor(c("Site A", "Site B")), x = 1:2) b <- tibble(site = factor(c("Site B", "Site C")), y = 3:4) joined <- full_join(a, b, by = "site") levels(joined$site) #> [1] "Site A" "Site B" "Site C" as.integer(a$site[a$site == "Site B"]) #> [1] 2 as.integer(b$site[b$site == "Site B"]) #> [1] 1 site_number <- factor(c("10", "2", "3")) as.numeric(site_number) #> [1] 1 2 3 as.numeric(as.character(site_number)) #> [1] 10 2 3 ``` ::: The joined key acquires the union of both level sets, in an order neither table chose, and `Site B` is code 2 in one table and code 1 in the other. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **`as.numeric()` on a factor returns its codes, not its labels.** A site number stored as a factor, `10`, `2`, `3`, becomes 1, 2, 3, because the codes follow the alphabetical order of the labels. Any join or calculation on those codes pairs rows by position in the level set, with the wrong labels and no error. Convert through `as.character()`, or better, keep identifiers and numbers out of factors altogether. ::: ### Exercises 1. Build `site` as a factor with the five protocol levels from the raw labels after `str_squish()` only, without `str_to_title()`. How many patients become `NA`, and under which raw spellings? 2. Fit `lm(event_30d ~ arm, data = trial)` with the default levels and with `fct_relevel(arm, "Usual care")`. Verify that the two `arm` coefficients are equal in size and opposite in sign, and say which one is the risk difference for home health against usual care. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} squished <- crf_raw |> mutate(site_f = factor(str_squish(site_raw), levels = site_levels)) sum(is.na(squished$site_f)) #> [1] 143 squished |> filter(is.na(site_f)) |> count(spelling = str_squish(site_raw)) #> # A tibble: 10 × 2 #> spelling n #> #> 1 SITE A 16 #> 2 SITE B 15 #> 3 SITE C 16 #> 4 SITE D 15 #> 5 SITE E 6 #> 6 site a 19 #> 7 site b 20 #> 8 site c 16 #> 9 site d 10 #> 10 site e 10 ``` ::: Every upper- and lower-case variant is refused, which is the point of declaring the levels: the `NA`s are a list of what the cleaning step still has to handle. With `factor()` and no levels, each of these spellings would have become a site of its own. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} lm_default <- lm(event_30d ~ arm, data = trial) lm_declared <- lm(event_30d ~ arm, data = trial |> mutate(arm = fct_relevel(arm, "Usual care"))) stopifnot(all.equal(unname(coef(lm_default)[2]), -unname(coef(lm_declared)[2]))) coef(lm_declared)[2] #> armHome health #> -0.02527255 ``` ::: With `Usual care` as the reference, the coefficient `armHome health` is the difference in the proportion with an event, home health minus usual care, among ascertained patients. A negative value favors home health. The default model reports the same number with the sign reversed, under the name `armUsual care`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** This chapter keeps categorical variables as character through reading, cleaning, and joining, and converts to factor only for modeling and plotting. What goes wrong if you convert at read time instead? **Answer.** Recoding becomes harder: assigning a value that is not already a level yields `NA` with a warning rather than the value you assigned, and `str_replace()` on a factor silently returns character. Joining becomes harder to reason about: two independently built factors rarely share a level set, the joined key acquires the union of both, and the codes behind the labels differ between tables, which bites as soon as anyone calls `as.integer()` on a key. A factor encodes a fixed set of categories and a reference level, which is exactly what a model needs and exactly what makes it brittle while the data are still moving. ::: ## Strings: structure from free text {#sec-types-strings} `medications.csv` has one row per discharge medication, and its `med_text` column records each as the prescriber typed it. The 16,927 rows use 57 distinct strings, mixing brand and generic names, `mg` with and without a space, upper and lower case, combination doses, units other than milligrams, and a dozen ways to say how often. The generic tour of `stringr` and regular expressions is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, chs. 14 and 15]; this section answers three questions a statistician asks of this column. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} meds <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "medications.csv"), col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character(), med_seq = col_integer(), med_text = col_character())) meds |> filter(patient_id == "0001") |> pull(med_text) #> [1] "Entresto 24-26 mg twice daily" #> [2] "metformin 1000mg bid with meals" #> [3] "Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg SL PRN chest pain" #> [4] "atorvastatin 80mg at bedtime" #> [5] "Digoxin 0.125 mg daily" #> [6] "Amiodarone 200 mg daily" #> [7] "Empagliflozin 10 mg daily" #> [8] "K-Dur 20 meq qd" #> [9] "Farxiga 10 mg QAM" ``` ::: ### Which drug? How many discharge prescriptions are for furosemide? The obvious pattern undercounts twice, once for case and once for the brand name: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c( case_sensitive = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text, "furosemide")), ignore_case = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text, regex("furosemide", ignore_case = TRUE))), with_brand = sum(str_detect(meds$med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix", ignore_case = TRUE))) ) #> case_sensitive ignore_case with_brand #> 142 590 735 ``` ::: Each count is a plausible number of prescriptions, and only the last is right. A drug question therefore starts with a lookup that names every spelling, brand and generic, for each class the analysis needs. For a heart-failure trial, three classes matter first: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) sacubitril-valsartan, and loop diuretics. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} meds <- meds |> mutate(drug_class = case_when( str_detect(med_text, regex("dapagliflozin|farxiga|empagliflozin|jardiance", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "SGLT2 inhibitor", str_detect(med_text, regex("sacubitril|entresto", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "ARNI", str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix|torsemide", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Loop diuretic" )) meds |> filter(!is.na(drug_class)) |> count(drug_class, med_text) #> # A tibble: 14 × 3 #> drug_class med_text n #> #> 1 ARNI Entresto 24-26 mg twice daily 254 #> 2 ARNI Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BID 238 #> 3 ARNI sacubitril-valsartan 97/103mg bid 254 #> 4 Loop diuretic FUROSEMIDE 80 MG QAM 153 #> 5 Loop diuretic Furosemide 20 mg daily 140 #> 6 Loop diuretic Furosemide 40 mg BID 155 #> 7 Loop diuretic Lasix 40 mg twice daily 145 #> 8 Loop diuretic Torsemide 20 mg daily 361 #> 9 Loop diuretic furosemide 40mg bid 142 #> 10 Loop diuretic torsemide 10mg qd 381 #> 11 SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily 384 #> 12 SGLT2 inhibitor Empagliflozin 10 mg daily 369 #> 13 SGLT2 inhibitor Farxiga 10 mg QAM 374 #> 14 SGLT2 inhibitor Jardiance 10mg qd 349 ``` ::: The cross-tabulation is the verification: every spelling that matched is listed beside its class, so a reader can see that `Farxiga` was counted and that nothing else was. ### What dose? The dose is a number, possibly with a decimal point, possibly a pair for a combination tablet (`49/51`, `24-26`), followed by a unit. The pattern below captures each part with a group, and `str_match()` returns one column per group: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dose_pattern <- regex( paste0("(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)", "(?:\\s*[/-]\\s*(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?))?", "\\s*(mg|mcg|meq|units)\\b"), ignore_case = TRUE ) dose_parts <- str_match(meds$med_text, dose_pattern) meds <- meds |> mutate( dose = as.numeric(dose_parts[, 2]), dose_2 = as.numeric(dose_parts[, 3]), unit = str_to_lower(dose_parts[, 4]), dose_mg = case_when(unit == "mg" ~ dose, unit == "mcg" ~ dose / 1000) ) meds |> count(unit) #> # A tibble: 4 × 2 #> unit n #> #> 1 mcg 1087 #> 2 meq 697 #> 3 mg 14443 #> 4 units 700 meds |> filter(!is.na(dose_2)) |> count(med_text, dose, dose_2) #> # A tibble: 3 × 4 #> med_text dose dose_2 n #> #> 1 Entresto 24-26 mg twice daily 24 26 254 #> 2 Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg BID 49 51 238 #> 3 sacubitril-valsartan 97/103mg bid 97 103 254 ``` ::: @tbl-regex-constructs reads the pattern piece by piece. | Piece | Matches | Why it is there | |---|---|---| | `\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?` | `40`, `0.4`, `12.5` | A dose with or without a decimal part; `(?: )` groups without capturing | | `(?:\\s*[/-]\\s*(...))?` | `/51`, `-26`, or nothing | The second component of a combination tablet, captured separately | | `\\s*` | Zero or more spaces | `40mg` and `40 mg` alike | | `(mg\|mcg\|meq\|units)` | The unit | Requiring a unit stops `q5min` from being read as a dose | | `\\b` | A word boundary | `mg` but not the start of a longer word | | `ignore_case = TRUE` | `MG`, `mEq` | Prescribers' capitalization varies | : The constructs in the dose pattern. In an R string each regular expression backslash is written twice. {#tbl-regex-constructs} ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A pattern that takes the first number misreads decimals, units, and combination doses, and returns a number every time.** `str_extract(x, "\\d+")` reads `0.4 mg` as 0, `12.5 mg` as 12, and `digoxin 125 mcg` as 125, which a later step treats as milligrams. `24-26 mg` is a combination tablet, 24 mg of sacubitril and 26 mg of valsartan, not a range and not 24 mg. Require the unit in the pattern, capture the decimal part, and convert units explicitly. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Every row should yield a dose and a unit from a known set, and two spellings of the same prescription should agree once units are converted: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} digoxin <- meds |> filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("digoxin", ignore_case = TRUE))) stopifnot( !anyNA(meds$dose), setequal(unique(meds$unit), c("mg", "mcg", "meq", "units")), n_distinct(digoxin$dose_mg) == 1 ) digoxin |> count(med_text, dose_mg) #> # A tibble: 2 × 3 #> med_text dose_mg n #> #> 1 Digoxin 0.125 mg daily 0.125 376 #> 2 digoxin 125 mcg QD 0.125 367 ``` ::: `0.125 mg` and `125 mcg` are the same dose, and the assertion says so. A first-number parse fails this check by a factor of a thousand. ::: ### How often? The frequency is written as Latin abbreviations with and without periods (`BID`, `b.i.d.`), as English (`twice daily`, `once a day`), and as timing (`QAM`, `qhs`, `at bedtime`). Remove the periods and the case, then map each phrase to doses per day. `PRN` (as needed) has no fixed daily count and stays `NA`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} freq_pattern <- paste( "\\bprn\\b", "\\bbid\\b", "twice daily", "\\btid\\b", "\\bqd\\b", "once daily", "once a day", "every day", "daily", "\\bqam\\b", "\\bqhs\\b", "at bedtime", sep = "|" ) meds <- meds |> mutate( freq_text = med_text |> str_to_lower() |> str_remove_all("\\."), freq_code = str_extract(freq_text, freq_pattern), per_day = case_when( freq_code == "prn" ~ NA_real_, freq_code %in% c("bid", "twice daily") ~ 2, freq_code == "tid" ~ 3, freq_code %in% c("qd", "once daily", "once a day", "every day", "daily", "qam", "qhs", "at bedtime") ~ 1 ) ) meds |> count(per_day, freq_code) #> # A tibble: 12 × 3 #> per_day freq_code n #> #> 1 1 at bedtime 587 #> 2 1 daily 4562 #> 3 1 every day 224 #> 4 1 once a day 263 #> 5 1 once daily 517 #> 6 1 qam 884 #> 7 1 qd 3428 #> 8 1 qhs 595 #> 9 2 bid 3225 #> 10 2 twice daily 399 #> 11 3 tid 1516 #> 12 NA prn 727 ``` ::: Two details carry the weight. `str_extract()` returns the leftmost match, so `twice daily` is found before the `daily` inside it; a `case_when()` that tested `str_detect(x, "daily")` first would call every twice-daily prescription once daily. And the word boundaries in `\\bqd\\b` and `\\bbid\\b` keep the codes from matching inside longer words. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Every row has a frequency code, and the only rows without a daily count are the as-needed ones: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot( !anyNA(meds$freq_code), all(is.na(meds$per_day) == (meds$freq_code == "prn")) ) ``` ::: ::: ### Exercises 3. Count *patients*, not prescriptions, discharged on an SGLT2 inhibitor in each arm. Join to `randomization.csv` with a declared relationship. 4. Compute the daily furosemide dose (`dose_mg * per_day`) for every furosemide prescription, in any spelling. Then recompute `per_day` with a `case_when()` that tests for `daily` before `twice daily`, and count the prescriptions, across all drugs, whose daily count changes. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sglt2_patients <- meds |> filter(drug_class == "SGLT2 inhibitor") |> distinct(patient_id) randomization |> left_join(sglt2_patients |> mutate(on_sglt2 = TRUE), by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |> mutate(on_sglt2 = coalesce(on_sglt2, FALSE)) |> count(arm, on_sglt2) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n), .by = arm) #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #> arm on_sglt2 n share #> #> 1 Home health FALSE 622 0.512 #> 2 Home health TRUE 594 0.488 #> 3 Usual care FALSE 583 0.479 #> 4 Usual care TRUE 633 0.521 ``` ::: `distinct()` comes first because a patient could hold two SGLT2 prescriptions; without it the join would be one-to-many and the declared relationship would refuse it. The shares in the two arms are within a few percentage points of each other, as randomization leads you to expect for a medication prescribed before the arm could influence it; a large difference would be worth a data query. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} meds |> filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix", ignore_case = TRUE))) |> mutate(daily_mg = dose_mg * per_day) |> count(med_text, daily_mg) #> # A tibble: 5 × 3 #> med_text daily_mg n #> #> 1 FUROSEMIDE 80 MG QAM 80 153 #> 2 Furosemide 20 mg daily 20 140 #> 3 Furosemide 40 mg BID 80 155 #> 4 Lasix 40 mg twice daily 80 145 #> 5 furosemide 40mg bid 80 142 wrong_order <- case_when( str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\bprn\\b") ~ NA_real_, str_detect(meds$freq_text, "daily") ~ 1, str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\bbid\\b|twice daily") ~ 2, str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\btid\\b") ~ 3, str_detect(meds$freq_text, "\\bqd\\b|once a day|every day|\\bqam\\b|\\bqhs\\b|at bedtime") ~ 1 ) sum(wrong_order != meds$per_day, na.rm = TRUE) #> [1] 399 meds |> filter(wrong_order != per_day) |> count(med_text) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #> med_text n #> #> 1 Entresto 24-26 mg twice daily 254 #> 2 Lasix 40 mg twice daily 145 ``` ::: Every `twice daily` prescription is halved, including the `Lasix 40 mg twice daily` rows, whose daily furosemide dose drops from 80 mg to 40 mg. No value is `NA` and no assertion on types fails; only the cross-tabulation of codes against counts shows it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** A colleague flags beta-blockers with `str_detect(med_text, "olol")`, because their generic names end that way. What does the flag count in this file, and what does it miss? **Answer.** Tabulate it against the spellings you know to be beta-blockers: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} meds |> filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("olol|coreg|toprol", ignore_case = TRUE))) |> count(med_text, flagged = str_detect(med_text, "olol")) #> # A tibble: 4 × 3 #> med_text flagged n #> #> 1 Coreg 25 mg b.i.d. FALSE 242 #> 2 Metoprolol succinate 50 mg daily TRUE 263 #> 3 Toprol XL 100 mg once daily FALSE 255 #> 4 metoprolol XL 25mg QD TRUE 227 ``` ::: The flag counts metoprolol written generically and misses carvedilol, whose name ends in `-dilol`, and the brands `Coreg` and `Toprol XL`. A suffix is a property of some names, not of the class. Build class flags from a lookup that names each drug, brand and generic, with `ignore_case = TRUE`, and print the matched spellings beside the class, as in `types-classes`, so a reader can see what was counted. ::: ## Dates: formats, ambiguity, and time {#sec-types-dates} The CRF export writes dates in four formats: `YYYY-MM-DD` at Sites A and B, `MM/DD/YYYY` at Site C, `DD-MON-YYYY` at Site D, and `YYYYMMDD` at Site E. @sec-wrangling parsed them site by site, and noted that a single call to `lubridate::parse_date_time()` with a list of formats returns a date for every row and gets some of them wrong. This section shows why, and how to find the rows at risk. The generic tour is in R for Data Science [@wickham2023r4ds, ch. 17]. ### One parser, several formats `parse_date_time()` accepts several `orders` and returns, for each value, a date under one of them. The per-site parse uses one order per site, as each site's codebook states: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} parse_site_date <- function(x, site) { case_when( site %in% c("Site A", "Site B", "Site E") ~ ymd(x, quiet = TRUE), site == "Site C" ~ mdy(x, quiet = TRUE), site == "Site D" ~ dmy(x, quiet = TRUE) ) } dates <- crf_raw |> transmute( site, discharge_raw = discharge_date, by_site = parse_site_date(discharge_date, site), one_call = as_date(parse_date_time(discharge_date, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"), quiet = TRUE)) ) dates |> count(site, wrong = by_site != one_call) #> # A tibble: 6 × 3 #> site wrong n #> #> 1 Site A FALSE 700 #> 2 Site B FALSE 571 #> 3 Site C FALSE 498 #> 4 Site D FALSE 223 #> 5 Site D TRUE 150 #> 6 Site E FALSE 290 dates |> filter(by_site != one_call) |> distinct() |> head(4) #> # A tibble: 4 × 4 #> site discharge_raw by_site one_call #> #> 1 Site D 03-FEB-2024 2024-02-03 2024-03-20 #> 2 Site D 05-FEB-2024 2024-02-05 2024-05-20 #> 3 Site D 10-FEB-2024 2024-02-10 2024-10-20 #> 4 Site D 01-MAR-2024 2024-03-01 2024-01-20 misread <- dates |> filter(by_site != one_call) |> summarize(n = n(), in_period = sum(between(one_call, min(dates$by_site), max(dates$by_site)))) misread #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #> n in_period #> #> 1 150 141 ``` ::: The single call parses every value and returns no `NA`, and every disagreement is at Site D. The rows shown are consistent with `03-FEB-2024` being read as month 03, with `FEB` skipped and `2024` split into a day, 20, and a two-digit year, 24. Of the 150 misread discharge dates, 141 fall inside the trial's enrollment period, so a range check on discharge dates catches only 9 of them. ### Ambiguous values Site D's failure comes from a format the orders did not describe well. Site C's risk is subtler: `03/04/2026` is a valid date under both `mdy` and `dmy`. `parse_date_time()` chooses an order by training on the whole vector, so the reading of one value depends on the order you list and on its neighbors: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} parse_date_time("03/04/2026", orders = c("mdy", "dmy")) #> [1] "2026-03-04 UTC" parse_date_time("03/04/2026", orders = c("dmy", "mdy")) #> [1] "2026-04-03 UTC" parse_date_time(c("03/04/2026", "25/04/2026"), orders = c("mdy", "dmy")) #> [1] "2026-04-03 UTC" "2026-04-25 UTC" ``` ::: Alone, with `mdy` listed first, the value is March 4. Beside a value that only `dmy` can read, the same value becomes April 3, under the same call and with no warning. A column's dates can therefore change when rows are added to it. The defense is to count the values a second convention would read differently: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ambiguous <- function(x) { as_mdy <- mdy(x, quiet = TRUE) as_dmy <- dmy(x, quiet = TRUE) !is.na(as_mdy) & !is.na(as_dmy) & as_mdy != as_dmy } crf_raw |> filter(site == "Site C") |> summarize(n = n(), ambiguous = sum(ambiguous(discharge_date))) #> # A tibble: 1 × 2 #> n ambiguous #> #> 1 498 207 ``` ::: Only Site C's codebook can resolve those values, which is why the parse is per site and the order is stated, not guessed. ::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'} **A multi-format parser never says it guessed.** `parse_date_time()` with several orders returns a date for every value it can read under any of them. Day-month swaps produce valid dates in the same month range, and a misread such as Site D's produces a plausible date in the same year. Parse each source with its single documented order, and count the ambiguous values before trusting any multi-order parse. ::: ::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'} > **Context.** A date column from three sources. Below are twenty > synthetic values in each source's format, and each source's > codebook line stating its format. > > **Constraints.** Parse each source with its single documented > order (`ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()`), not `parse_date_time()` with > several orders and not nested `ifelse()`. Use `quiet = TRUE` and > count failures explicitly. > > **Criteria.** Return a function `parse_source_date(x, source)` and > a check that reports, per source, the number of `NA`s and the > number of values that `mdy()` and `dmy()` would read as different > dates. *Failure mode.* The model's default answer is `parse_date_time(x, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"))`, often called the robust choice. It returns a date for every value, so an `NA` count finds nothing, and it misreads exactly the values this section counts. *Check.* Compare the model's parse with the per-site parse row by row, as in `types-dates`; any disagreement is a misread by one of them. Send synthetic values in the source's format, not real dates of birth (@sec-ai-governance). ::: ### Excel serial dates A date column from a spreadsheet may arrive as five-digit numbers, Excel's count of days from its own origin. Converting with `as.Date()` counts from R's origin instead: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} as.Date(45405) #> [1] "2094-04-25" as.Date(45405, origin = "1899-12-30") #> [1] "2024-04-23" janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(45405) #> [1] "2024-04-23" ``` ::: `as.Date(45405)` is a valid date seventy years from now, and nothing about it is `NA`.[^excel-origin] Any column whose name says date and whose values are numbers is a bug until shown otherwise; the assertion is a range check against the study period. [^excel-origin]: Since R 4.3.0, `as.Date()` on a number uses 1970-01-01 as the origin when none is given; earlier versions required an `origin`. The Excel origin of 1899-12-30, rather than 1900-01-01, absorbs Excel's treatment of 1900 as a leap year, which holds for dates after February 1900 in the default Windows date system. ### Time zones and daylight saving HF-HOME records dates without times, which is the safe case for daily-resolution analyses. Device data, electronic health record audit logs, and infusion pumps record date-times, and a date-time without a time zone is ambiguous: Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), the site's zone, or the zone of the server that wrote it? `lubridate` parses a date-time without a zone as UTC; base R uses the session's zone. Say which: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") t #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 PDT" with_tz(t, "UTC") #> [1] "2026-04-23 21:30:00 UTC" force_tz(t, "UTC") #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ``` ::: `with_tz()` changes the displayed zone without changing the instant; `force_tz()` changes the instant by declaring that the clock reading was always in the new zone. Confusing them shifts times by the offset between the zones, here seven hours. Daylight-saving transitions add a second trap. In most US time zones, daylight-saving time began at 2:00 a.m. on March 8, 2026, so an interval that starts at noon the day before crosses it: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} start <- ymd_hms("2026-03-07 12:00:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") start + days(1) #> [1] "2026-03-08 12:00:00 PDT" start + hours(24) #> [1] "2026-03-08 12:00:00 PDT" start + dhours(24) #> [1] "2026-03-08 13:00:00 PDT" ``` ::: `days(1)` and `hours(24)` are both *periods*: they advance the clock, and land at noon on March 8. `dhours(24)` is a *duration* of exactly 86,400 seconds, and lands at 1:00 p.m., because the night of the transition was only 23 hours long. Use a period for a calendar notion of a day and a duration for elapsed time, whichever the analysis requires. ### Exercises 5. Parse `dob` per site and verify it against `demographics.csv`. Then parse it with the single `parse_date_time()` call of `types-dates`, and count the dates of birth it gets wrong and how many of those fall after the patient's discharge date. 6. Count the ambiguous dates of birth at Site C. For one of them, show the date `mdy()` and `dmy()` each return. 7. Create a date-time in `America/Los_Angeles` and convert it to UTC with `with_tz()` and with `force_tz()`. Explain the difference, and say when each is the right call. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dob <- crf_raw |> transmute( patient_id, site, by_site = parse_site_date(dob, site), one_call = as_date(parse_date_time(dob, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"), quiet = TRUE)), discharge = parse_site_date(discharge_date, site) ) stopifnot(identical(dob$by_site, demographics$dob[match(dob$patient_id, demographics$patient_id)])) dob_wrong <- dob |> filter(by_site != one_call) |> summarize(wrong = n(), after_discharge = sum(one_call > discharge), .by = site) dob_wrong #> # A tibble: 1 × 3 #> site wrong after_discharge #> #> 1 Site D 125 112 ``` ::: The per-site parse agrees with the answer key for every patient. The single call misreads only Site D's dates of birth. Of its 125 misreads, 112 place the birth after the discharge, which a range check catches; the other 13 are plausible ages and are caught by nothing but the comparison. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} site_c_dob <- crf_raw |> filter(site == "Site C") |> pull(dob) sum(ambiguous(site_c_dob)) #> [1] 176 example <- site_c_dob[ambiguous(site_c_dob)][1] c(raw = example, mdy = format(mdy(example)), dmy = format(dmy(example))) #> raw mdy dmy #> "03/07/1952" "1952-03-07" "1952-07-03" ``` ::: Site C's codebook says `MM/DD/YYYY`, so `mdy()` is right. Nothing in the values says so: for each ambiguous date, both readings are real dates. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t <- ymd_hms("2026-04-23 14:30:00", tz = "America/Los_Angeles") with_tz(t, "UTC") #> [1] "2026-04-23 21:30:00 UTC" force_tz(t, "UTC") #> [1] "2026-04-23 14:30:00 UTC" ``` ::: `with_tz` preserves the moment and relabels it; `force_tz` preserves the digits and moves the moment. Use `with_tz` when combining data recorded in different zones, and `force_tz` only to repair a timestamp that was stamped with the wrong zone to begin with. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** Three things go wrong with dates in this chapter: a multi-format column parsed with one `parse_date_time()` call, an Excel serial number read with `as.Date()`, and `days(1)` used where a duration was meant. Which will your code tell you about? **Answer.** None of them. The single parse returns a date for every Site D value and is wrong for some; an `NA` count finds nothing. The Excel number becomes a valid date seventy years out. The daylight saving case returns a correct answer to a different question: `days(1)` gives the same clock time the next day, `dhours(24)` the instant 24 hours later, and R cannot know which you meant. A bug that produces `NA` is cheap; a bug that produces a plausible date is expensive, and the comparison against a per-source parse or a range check is the assertion that makes it loud (Habit 8). ::: ## Worked example: a typed patient table {#sec-types-worked} The script below gathers the chapter into one patient-level table: site and sex as factors with declared levels, the discharge date parsed per site, the arm with its reference set, and three medication summaries. It reuses `crf_typed`, `parse_site_date()`, and the parsed `meds` from the sections above. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} med_summary <- meds |> summarize( n_meds = n(), on_sglt2 = any(drug_class == "SGLT2 inhibitor", na.rm = TRUE), on_arni = any(drug_class == "ARNI", na.rm = TRUE), loop_mg_day = sum( if_else(str_detect(med_text, regex("furosemide|lasix", ignore_case = TRUE)), dose_mg * per_day, 0) ), .by = patient_id ) patients <- crf_typed |> transmute( patient_id, site, sex, discharge_date = parse_site_date(discharge_date, as.character(site)) ) |> left_join(randomization |> select(patient_id, arm), by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one", unmatched = "error") |> left_join(med_summary, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |> mutate( arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Usual care", "Home health")), across(c(n_meds, loop_mg_day), \(x) coalesce(x, 0)), across(c(on_sglt2, on_arni), \(x) coalesce(x, FALSE)) ) glimpse(patients) #> Rows: 2,432 #> Columns: 9 #> $ patient_id "0001", "0002", "0003", "0004", "0005", "0006", "0007",… #> $ site Site B, Site E, Site E, Site B, Site A, Site A, Site B,… #> $ sex F, F, F, M, F, M, M, M, M, M, F, M, M, F, M, M, F, M, M… #> $ discharge_date 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-02-01, 2024-0… #> $ arm Home health, Home health, Usual care, Usual care, Usual… #> $ n_meds 9, 8, 10, 5, 5, 3, 5, 7, 9, 10, 5, 5, 9, 8, 5, 6, 4, 6,… #> $ on_sglt2 TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, TRU… #> $ on_arni TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FA… #> $ loop_mg_day 0, 0, 80, 0, 80, 0, 80, 0, 20, 0, 0, 0, 80, 0, 0, 80, 0… patients |> summarize(n = n(), sglt2 = mean(on_sglt2), arni = mean(on_arni), furosemide = mean(loop_mg_day > 0), .by = arm) |> arrange(arm) #> # A tibble: 2 × 5 #> arm n sglt2 arni furosemide #> #> 1 Usual care 1216 0.521 0.318 0.295 #> 2 Home health 1216 0.488 0.295 0.309 ``` ::: Two judgments are written into the code. Patients with no medication rows get `n_meds = 0` and `FALSE` flags, which is the codebook's meaning of an absent row; in a file where absence could mean 'not recorded', the right value would be `NA`. And `loop_mg_day` counts furosemide only, because torsemide is about twice as potent per milligram and adding the two would mix units of effect; a dose-equivalence rule belongs in the analysis plan, not in a cleaning script's arithmetic. ::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'} Confirm the types and levels, and check the medication count against the clean `baseline.csv`, which records each patient's number of discharge medications: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} baseline <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"), col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE) stopifnot( nrow(patients) == nrow(randomization), identical(levels(patients$arm), c("Usual care", "Home health")), identical(levels(patients$site), site_levels), inherits(patients$discharge_date, "Date"), !anyNA(patients$discharge_date), all(patients$n_meds == baseline$discharge_med_count[match(patients$patient_id, baseline$patient_id)]) ) sum(patients$n_meds == 0) #> [1] 2 ``` ::: The last assertion checks the string work end to end: a patient whose medication rows were lost or duplicated would fail it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'} **Question.** The worked example converts `arm` to a factor at the end of the script, after both joins. Why not at the start, when `randomization.csv` is read? **Answer.** Here the arm is not a join key, so converting early would do no harm; the reason is where the declaration sits. Converting at the end keeps every column that a join, filter, or recode touches in its plain type, and puts the reference level beside the analysis that depends on it, where a reviewer looks for it. Had `arm` been a key, or been recoded after the read, an early factor would have needed its levels managed at every step, and a join would have given it the union of two level sets. ::: ## Rules of thumb 1. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Keep categories as character until the model, then declare the levels and the reference in writing, and assert them. 2. **Habit 8: a parser that always returns a value cannot tell you it guessed.** A first-number regex, a multi-order date parse, and an Excel serial date all produce plausible values; compare against a second, stricter reading and count the disagreements. 3. **Habit 12: every model output is a hypothesis until verified.** A model's regular expression or date parser is checked on the full column, with a cross-tabulation of what it matched. ## Cumulative practice 8. *Cumulative (uses @sec-joins).* Add each patient's discharge potassium from `labs.csv` (visit `-01`, test `K`) to `patients`, with a declared relationship, after handling the duplicated discharge potassium that @sec-wrangling found. Flag the patients discharged on a potassium supplement (`K-Dur`, `KCl`, or `potassium chloride`, in any case) and compare their median discharge potassium with everyone else's. 9. *On your own work (no key).* Write a function that takes any character column and returns each value with its count and proportion, and use it to audit the categorical variables in a recent analysis of yours. Report every level you did not expect. ::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 8'} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} labs <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "labs.csv"), col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()), show_col_types = FALSE) discharge_k <- labs |> filter(str_ends(visit_id, "-01"), test_code == "K") |> distinct() |> filter(n() == 1, .by = patient_id) |> select(patient_id, k_discharge = value) k_supplement <- meds |> filter(str_detect(med_text, regex("k-dur|\\bkcl\\b|potassium chloride", ignore_case = TRUE))) |> distinct(patient_id) |> mutate(on_k = TRUE) with_k <- patients |> left_join(discharge_k, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |> left_join(k_supplement, by = "patient_id", relationship = "one-to-one") |> mutate(on_k = coalesce(on_k, FALSE)) stopifnot(nrow(with_k) == nrow(patients)) with_k |> summarize(n = n(), missing_k = sum(is.na(k_discharge)), median_k = median(k_discharge, na.rm = TRUE), .by = on_k) #> # A tibble: 2 × 4 #> on_k n missing_k median_k #> #> 1 TRUE 697 0 4.3 #> 2 FALSE 1735 1 4.3 ``` ::: `distinct()` removes the exact duplicate, and the `n() == 1` filter sets aside the potassium that was re-run with a different value, as @sec-wrangling did, so that patient's potassium is missing rather than invented; the `missing_k` column shows it. The orphan patient in `labs.csv` never reaches `patients`, because the left join keeps only randomized patients. Whether supplemented patients differ is descriptive here; potassium supplements are prescribed in response to low potassium, so any difference is confounded by indication. ::: ## Cheat sheet | Task | Code | Guards against | |---|---|---| | Collapse spellings to levels | `fct_collapse(x, F = c("F", "f", "2"), M = c(...))` | Several codes for one category | | Rename levels | `fct_recode(x, Female = "F")` | Codes in tables and figures | | Declare the level set | `factor(x, levels = site_levels)` | Variant spellings becoming categories | | Set the reference | `fct_relevel(arm, "Usual care")` | Effects reported in the wrong direction | | Order by frequency or value | `fct_infreq(x)`, `fct_reorder(x, y, median)` | Alphabetical order in plots | | Lump rare levels | `fct_lump_min(x, min = 10)` | Unstable estimates for tiny groups | | Count levels, including empty | `fct_count(x)` | Dropped or unexpected levels | | Detect, ignoring case | `str_detect(x, regex("lasix", ignore_case = TRUE))` | Undercounts from capitalization | | Capture parts | `str_match(x, "(\\d+(?:\\.\\d+)?)\\s*(mg\|mcg)")` | First-number parsing | | Normalize text | `str_to_lower()`, `str_squish()`, `str_remove_all(x, "\\.")` | Spellings that differ only in form | | Parse one known format | `ymd()`, `mdy()`, `dmy()` | Guessed conventions | | Find ambiguous dates | `!is.na(mdy(x)) & !is.na(dmy(x)) & mdy(x) != dmy(x)` | Silent day-month swaps | | Excel serial dates | `janitor::excel_numeric_to_date(x)` | Dates seventy years off | | Change displayed zone | `with_tz(t, "UTC")` | Mixing zones across sources | | Repair a wrong zone | `force_tz(t, "UTC")` | Timestamps stamped in the wrong zone | | Calendar day versus elapsed time | `days(1)` versus `ddays(1)` | One-hour errors at daylight-saving transitions | | Add months safely | `d %m+% months(3)` | Invalid dates such as February 30 | : Factors, strings, and dates at a glance. {#tbl-types-cheat-sheet} ## Further reading - [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 14 to 17: strings, regular expressions, factors, and dates and times. - [@bryan2019stat545] Chapters 10 to 13, detailed type-specific coverage. - [@grolemund2011dates], the `lubridate` paper, for the date and time-zone handling in this chapter. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-14} 1. Before R 4.0, `read.csv()` and `data.frame()` converted character columns to factors by default. Levels appeared where a character string was expected, for example as merge keys, new values could not be assigned without first adding a level, and `as.numeric()` on a numeric-looking column returned codes rather than values. R 4.0 made `FALSE` the default, and the old default now matters only when reading older code. 2. `str_detect(string, pattern)` returns a logical vector of the same length as `string`: `TRUE` where the pattern matched, `FALSE` elsewhere. `str_extract()` returns a character vector, the first matching substring per input, or `NA` where there was no match. `str_detect()` is for filtering and flagging; `str_extract()` is for pulling out parts. 3. `parse_date_time(x, orders = c('ymd', 'mdy', 'Bdy'))` parses all three. A fourth value `'03/04/2026'` is valid as March 4 and as April 3. With only `mdy` among the slash orders it is read as March 4, but if `dmy` were also listed, the reading would depend on the order of the list and on the other values in the vector, with no warning. Parse each source with its single documented order, and count the values that a second convention would read differently.
